The scholiast, who explains it by διατόρει [bore through], διακόμιζε [carry through], seems to have read the simple form τέτραινε [bore]: hence Blomfield conjectured δὲ σῶν [through your], Bamberger δ᾽ ἔσω [and within], Hermann τέ σοι [and for you]. The sense is: make it penetrate through the ears into the innermost recess. Wordsworth compared Soph. fr. 737 δι᾿ ὐτὸς ἔρχεται τρυπωμένου [it goes through the ear being pierced].
Hearing such things, write them in your mind, and bore the word through your ears with a quiet foundation of the mind.

I compose. It is taken in a novel sense of adding.

Hermann observed that it could more fittingly be expressed by ἐντίθησι [he puts in]. The meaning of composing can be preserved if παιδός μόρον [the child's death] is taken as θρήνον περὶ παιδὸς μόρου [a lament about the child's death], as συνθεῖναι ποίημα [to compose a poem] and λόγον [a speech] are said, which Phrynichus noted in Bekk. where Hermann says: “σύρδην [in a long line] is said of great forces, which in long trains as it were flood the roads: which metaphor Aeschylus uses in v. 89 ff., saying μεγάλῳ ῥεύματι φωτῶν [with a great stream of men] and ἄμαχον κύμα θαλάσσης [an irresistible wave of the sea].”

It is said differently in Rhesus 56 πρὶν τὸν Ἀργείων στρατὸν | σύρδην ἅπαντα τῷδ᾽ ἀνάλῶσαι δορί [before destroying the whole Argive army in a long line with this spear]. A third example of this word is brought from Nicetas Chon. Ann. 7 p. 119 c. ἀνέμου πνεύσαντος καὶ θῖνὰ βαθεῖαν ἐκ τῆς ἐκεῖσε ψαμμώδους μετεωρίσαντος γῆς σύρδην ἐμπίπτουσαν [when a wind blew and raised a deep sandbank from the sandy ground there, falling in a long line]. Alciphro 1, 23 said φύρδην φερόμενοι ἄνεμοι [winds borne in confusion], where the Florentine codex has σύρδην [in a long line].
Babylon, rich in gold, sends a mixed crowd in a long line.
